import numpy as np
grp2 = np.array([g for g,_ in t1m]); math2 = np.isin(grp2,['G1','G2','G4']); non2 = np.isin(grp2,['G3','G5'])
prev_c=prev_l=None; rows=[]
for l in range(0,27):
    H=np.load(f'/work/fwd_2/hidden_{l}.npy', mmap_mode='r')
    C=np.stack([np.asarray(H[k,4:lens2[k]-5],dtype=np.float32)[:,keep].mean(0) for k in range(len(lens2))])
    Lp=np.stack([np.asarray(H[k,lens2[k]-1],dtype=np.float32)[keep] for k in range(len(lens2))])
    dc=C[math2].mean(0)-C[non2].mean(0); dl=Lp[math2].mean(0)-Lp[non2].mean(0)
    rc=np.linalg.norm(dc)/np.linalg.norm(C,axis=1).mean(); rl=np.linalg.norm(dl)/np.linalg.norm(Lp,axis=1).mean()
    cc = '' if prev_c is None else f"{dc@prev_c/np.linalg.norm(dc)/np.linalg.norm(prev_c):+.2f}"
    cl = '' if prev_l is None else f"{dl@prev_l/np.linalg.norm(dl)/np.linalg.norm(prev_l):+.2f}"
    rows.append(f"L{l:2d} content: rel|dm| {rc:.3f} cos(prev) {cc:>5} | lastP: rel|dm| {rl:.3f} cos(prev) {cl:>5}")
    prev_c, prev_l = dc, dl
print('\n'.join(rows))

The model reads the numbers and computes correctly, but chooses the wrong *relation*, as in "20 + 70" where the problem needs "6×20 + 2×70". A corruption of how relational words ("each", "per", "times", "half", "more") are processed would produce exactly this.

Teacher-forced reference solutions can test it. At operator positions, a model with that defect would put low probability on the correct operator and prefer the wrong one, especially "+" where "×" is needed. The screening texts are prompt plus reference solution with the annotations stripped ("2 * 7 = 14", "1050 / 14 = 75"), so operators appear as ordinary tokens between numbers.

From pass 8 (top-20 predictions on 150 DEV reference solutions) I will look at every position where the reference writes an arithmetic operator (+, −, *, /, ×). The model is uncertain whether an operator or a unit word comes next, so I restrict its top-20 distribution to the operator tokens alone. This isolates the *relational* choice: given that an operation follows, does the model pick the right one?

I report, per correct operator, how often the model's preferred operator matches and which wrong operator it prefers instead. Systematic substitutions, such as "+" preferred where "*" is correct well beyond the reverse, would point to a corrupted relation-processing mechanism. High, symmetric operator accuracy would put the deficit upstream, in which quantities get combined.

Operator choice is not systematically corrupted. Given the reference context, the model's preferred operator is correct 81% of the time for "+", 89% for "−", 70% for "×" and 80% for "/". The errors are spread over all alternatives, for example "×" confused with "−" (20) and "/" (17), not "+" (9). That is ordinary uncertainty, not a broken relation word, so the deficit lies in which quantities and relations the model sets up.
